title: Consistency: what you give up, and CAP in plain words
story:
The lineage matters here, because the slogan is remembered and the result is not.

The idea's first publication was Fox and Brewer's 1999 HotOS paper, Harvest, yield, and scalable tolerant systems, which introduced harvest — the fraction of the data reflected in a response — and yield — the fraction of requests answered successfully — as metrics for graceful degradation. Note that both are fractions. The framing was quantitative before it became a three-letter choice.

Then on Wednesday 19 July 2000, Brewer delivered the keynote Towards Robust Distributed Systems at the 19th Annual ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing. It proposed that only two of three properties can be obtained simultaneously: consistency, meaning distributed components agree on the value of shared state; availability, meaning the ability to respond to user requests; and tolerance to network partitions, meaning the ability to keep operating when communication fails. He drew on his theoretical work at Berkeley together with what he had seen running Inktomi, and the talk is widely credited with opening the field to designs offering different tradeoffs.

He posed it as a conjecture. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch of MIT proved it in 2002, in ACM SIGACT News, and their proof is more interesting than the slogan it licensed. They established two results, not one: a strong impossibility result for asynchronous networks, which have no clocks, and a weaker one for partially synchronous networks, which have unsynchronised clocks measuring time at the same rate — and in that second, more realistic setting, a practical compromise between consistency and availability is achievable. They also use the word atomic rather than consistent, which is the more precise term, since consistency already means something else in the transactional sense.

The part almost always dropped is that Brewer himself reframed it. In 2012 he published CAP twelve years later: how the rules have changed, observing that partition tolerance is not really a property that can be traded away, because a designer does not get to choose whether the network has partitions. Cables are cut, switches reboot, routers drop packets. The design problem is how to trade consistency against availability when a partition occurs — which means the popular reading, pick two of three, misdescribes the thing its own author was describing.

So when a link between two regions drops, the choice is forced and it is about failure, not about architecture. Refuse writes on the side that cannot coordinate, returning an error rather than risking divergence — the right answer for a ledger or an inventory decrement. Or accept the writes and reconcile afterwards.

Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper is the canonical worked example of the second, and worth reading for how far it goes. It targets the design space of an always writeable store by pushing conflict resolution to read time, so that writes are never rejected, on the grounds that a customer must be able to add an item to a cart even during partial network failures or data centre outages. Versions are tracked with vector clocks, each a list of node and counter pairs, and when branches cannot be reconciled automatically the store hands all the leaves back for the application to merge. For the cart the merge is the union of the conflicting versions — so a deleted item can reappear, and nothing is lost. That is the shape of the bill: availability was bought, and it was paid for in a user-visible semantic that somebody had to decide was acceptable.

problem.name: The partition decision
problem.shape: Two nodes that replicate data cannot reach each other, and a write arrives.
tell: a design claims immediate agreement and continuous availability together
someone proposes to decline partition tolerance
there is no stated behaviour for the case where replicas cannot communicate
conflicting versions exist and no one has decided how they merge
problem.move: Treat the partition as given and decide in advance what happens during one. Either refuse the write on the side that cannot coordinate and return an error, or accept it and specify the merge — and if you accept, write down the user-visible consequence of the merge rule, because there always is one.
problem.invariant: Partition tolerance is not a property you select; the network supplies it. What you select is what fails when a partition happens.
problem.breaks: The slogan overstates the result in the setting people actually build in. The strong impossibility holds for asynchronous networks with no clocks; in partially synchronous networks — unsynchronised clocks running at the same rate — a practical compromise between consistency and availability is achievable, so 'pick two' is a heuristic rather than the theorem.

cost.time: consistency costs at least one round trip between nodes on every write, which is a latency floor set by geography
cost.space: availability costs per-version metadata and merge logic, and the metadata grows with the number of writers
cost.beats: a single node, which has no partition to tolerate and no availability either, and synchronous replication everywhere, which converts every network hiccup into an outage

worked.problem: Why is 'I choose consistency and availability, and I will do without partition tolerance' not an available answer?
worked.reasoning:
Because partitions are not one of the things being chosen. Cables are cut, switches reboot and routers drop packets, so the network supplies partitions whether or not the design acknowledges them. Declining partition tolerance does not remove partitions; it removes the plan for them, and a system without a plan still behaves somehow during one — usually by doing both bad things at once, serving stale reads and rejecting writes, with nobody having decided that.

Brewer made this point himself, which is why it is worth stating firmly. His 2012 retrospective observes that the tradeoff is more subtle than the slogan and that partition tolerance is not really a property that can be traded away, because a designer cannot choose whether the network has partitions. He reframed the design problem as how to trade consistency against availability when a partition occurs. The popular reading — pick two of three — misdescribes what its own author was describing.

So the real question is what happens on the side of the partition that cannot coordinate. Refusing the write preserves consistency and sacrifices availability for those users, which is correct where divergence is more expensive than an error: a ledger entry, an inventory decrement, anything where two conflicting truths cannot later be merged into one. Accepting the write preserves availability and sacrifices consistency, which is correct where an error costs more than a reconciliation.

Dynamo is the worked example of the second choice and it is more instructive than the summary suggests. It targets the design space of an always writeable store by pushing conflict resolution to read time, so writes are never rejected — the motivating case being that a customer must be able to add an item to a cart even during partial network failures or data centre outages. Versions are tracked with vector clocks, each a list of node and counter pairs, and where branches cannot be reconciled automatically the store returns all the leaves and the application merges them. For the cart, the merge rule is union.

Which produces the detail I would put at the centre of an answer: under union, a deleted item can reappear. Nothing is lost, and that is the guarantee they wanted — but 'nothing is lost' and 'the cart is correct' are different statements, and the gap between them is where the availability was paid for. Choosing availability is not a way of avoiding the consistency problem; it relocates it into application semantics that a user can observe.

One correction to the usual telling, because it changes how much the result can bear. The strong impossibility proof is for asynchronous networks, which have no clocks. Gilbert and Lynch also proved a weaker result for partially synchronous networks — unsynchronised clocks measuring time at the same rate — where a practical compromise between consistency and availability is achievable. Real systems are in the second category. So the theorem does not say that a partitioned system must abandon one property entirely; it bounds what can be guaranteed, and the engineering lives in the compromise it leaves open.

problem.practice: Take a replicated store you depend on and find its documented behaviour during a partition. If the documentation describes throughput and durability but not what a write does when replicas cannot see each other, you have found the decision nobody made.

beats.broke: Systems were described as delivering immediate agreement, continuous availability and survival of a severed link at the same time — three guarantees, where at most two are available.
beats.fix: Partition tolerance is not a choice, so the real decision is what happens during a partition: refuse the write and stay consistent, or accept it and reconcile afterwards.
beats.cost: Consistency costs a round trip between nodes on every write. Availability costs version tracking and application-level merge logic, and the merge rule has consequences a user can see.

interview.q: Why is 'I choose consistency and availability, and I will do without partition tolerance' not an available answer, and how does Dynamo illustrate the alternative?
interview.trap: Arguing that it becomes available if the network is reliable enough — five nines, a dedicated link, a single region. Reliability changes how often a partition happens, not whether the system has defined behaviour when one does.
interview.answer:
Because partitions are not among the things being chosen. Cables are cut, switches reboot, routers drop packets — the network supplies partitions whether or not the design acknowledges them. The real question is what the side that cannot coordinate does with a write. Refusing it keeps consistency and drops availability for those users, which is right where divergence costs more than an error — a ledger entry, an inventory decrement, anything where two truths cannot later be merged.
